question: A rectangular box \(\mathcal{P}\) has distinct edge lengths \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c.\) The sum of the lengths of all \(12\) edges of \(\mathcal{P}\) is \(13,\) the sum of the areas of all \(6\) faces of \(\mathcal{P}\) is \(\frac{11}{2},\) and the volume of \(\mathcal{P}\) is \(\frac{1}{2}.\) What is the length of the longest interior diagonal connecting two vertices of \(\mathcal{P}?\)
solution:
The interior diagonal depends on \(a^2+b^2+c^2\), and the edge and face totals let us find this sum without solving for the individual edge lengths.

There are four edges of each length, so
\[
4(a+b+c)=13,
\qquad a+b+c=\frac{13}{4}.
\]
The faces come in three equal-area pairs, giving
\[
2(ab+bc+ca)=\frac{11}{2},
\qquad ab+bc+ca=\frac{11}{4}.
\]
To relate these quantities to the diagonal, let \(A\) and \(B\) be opposite vertices of a bottom face with side lengths \(a\) and \(b\). Let \(C\) be the vertex directly above \(B\), with \(BC=c\). The Pythagorean theorem gives \(AB^2=a^2+b^2\). Since \(BC\) is perpendicular to the bottom face, triangle \(ABC\) is right at \(B\), so the interior diagonal \(AC\) satisfies
\[
AC^2=AB^2+BC^2=a^2+b^2+c^2.
\]
Expanding the square of the sum now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a^2+b^2+c^2
&=(a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca)\\
&=\left(\frac{13}{4}\right)^2-2\left(\frac{11}{4}\right)\\
&=\frac{169-88}{16}
=\frac{81}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All interior diagonals of a rectangular box have this same length. Thus the requested length is
\[
\boxed{AC=\sqrt{\frac{81}{16}}=\frac94},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
